64.title: Kumbhakarna wakes
64.hook: the giant who sleeps six months
64.howItsDone: Kumbhakarna's waking is a favorite, often comic scene in Ramlila plays and children's retellings, and in everyday Indian speech a heavy sleeper is sometimes teasingly called a Kumbhakarna.

segments.voice: Last time: Lakshmana falls, and Hanuman flies the length of India before dawn. Your line was fly. Did you show up for someone without calculating? Day sixty-four.

Everybody knows someone who's impossible to wake up. The teenager at noon. The uncle on the sofa after lunch. Now meet the champion. Ravana is losing. His generals are dead, his city is surrounded, and he's out of options except one. Deep in the palace, his brother is asleep. Kumbhakarna, a giant so huge that when he stands up, the story says, he's like a mountain walking. And he sleeps for months at a time. So Ravana sends servants to wake him. Today's week starts with the hardest alarm clock in literature.
screen: `IMPOSSIBLE TO WAKE.` → `RAVANA IS OUT OF OPTIONS.` → `THE GIANT ASLEEP IN THE PALACE.`

segments.voice: How do you wake a giant? In Valmiki, it's almost comic. Thousands of demons pile up mountains of food and jars of drink by his nose so the smell will reach him. They beat drums, blow conches, shout, roar. They hit him with clubs and hammers. They drive elephants over his body. Finally, he yawns, and wakes up hungry. Why does he sleep like that? The tradition tells it this way: long ago he did fierce austerities, and the gods were terrified of what he'd ask for. When the creator god Brahma offered him a boon, the goddess of speech, Sarasvati, entered his mouth, and instead of what he meant to ask, out came a wish for sleep. In later tellings it's a slip of one syllable: he meant to ask for Indra's throne, indrasana, and said nidrasana, a bed of sleep. And then comes the surprise. Kumbhakarna wakes up, hears what Ravana has done, and tells him straight: you were wrong to take Sita. You ignored good advice. This is your own doing. The giant is the one with the clear head. And then he goes out and fights for his brother anyway. Loyalty, even to the wrong cause. He's terrifying on the battlefield, crushing monkeys by the dozen, until Rama's arrows finally bring him down, and his fall shakes the earth. Think about the cost of that alarm clock: drums, elephants, a city's worth of food. Some things in us are asleep for good reason. A temper. An old grief. A strength we don't use. Waking them takes enormous effort, and once they're up, they don't go back to bed easily. So if you're going to wake a giant, know what you want it for.
screen: `DRUMS, ELEPHANTS, MOUNTAINS OF FOOD.` · `ONE SLIP OF THE TONGUE: SLEEP.` · `THE GIANT TELLS HIM HE WAS WRONG.` · `THEN FIGHTS FOR HIM ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of something big in you that's been asleep. Maybe it's anger you've kept down for years. Maybe it's grief you haven't let yourself feel. Maybe it's a gift, a strength, an ambition you've put to bed. Don't wake it. Just walk up to it, in your mind, and look at it sleeping. How big is it? What would it want if it woke up? What would you want it for? Just look, and breathe, and let it sleep for now. The bell holds the time.
Kumbhakarna wakes. Ravana's giant brother, roused by drums and elephants, who tells the truth and then fights for him anyway.
Your line: wake it carefully. Today, before you stir up an old fight or an old feeling, ask what you want it for. Day sixty-four.

65.title: Ravana rides out
65.howItsDone: At Dussehra, many communities in north India burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana, and teachers often use the ten heads to speak about the inner faults that keep returning; the Shiva Tandava Stotram, attributed to Ravana, is widely chanted by devotees of Shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna wakes, the giant who told his brother the truth and fought for him anyway. Your line was wake it carefully. Did you leave one old fight asleep? Day sixty-five.

For the whole war, Ravana has sent other people. Generals. Sons. His giant brother. One by one, they've fallen. Kumbhakarna is gone. And now even Indrajit, his great son, the master of illusion, has been killed by Lakshmana. There's nobody left to send. So the king of Lanka puts on his armor, climbs into his chariot, and rides out through the gates himself. Ten heads. Twenty arms. A bow in several hands at once. After all these weeks, the serial finally brings the two of them face to face: Rama on foot, Ravana in the chariot. Today: the king with ten heads.
screen: `EVERYONE HE SENT HAS FALLEN.` → `THE GATES OPEN.` → `FACE TO FACE, AT LAST.`

segments.voice: It's easy to make Ravana a cartoon, and the Ramayana doesn't. He's a great scholar in the tradition, learned in the Vedas. He's a fierce devotee of Shiva; a famous hymn to Shiva's dance, the Shiva Tandava Stotram, is traditionally said to be his. He plays the veena. He's brave, and he is a real king to his people. And he took another man's wife by force and wouldn't give her back when everyone he trusted begged him to. That's the tragedy: all that greatness, bent around one refusal. Even his name carries a story. In the tradition, he once tried to lift Shiva's mountain, Kailasa, and Shiva pressed it down with one toe, pinning him. Ravana roared so loudly the worlds shook, and Shiva, in the Uttara Kanda's telling, named him Ravana: the one who made the worlds cry out. Now the fight. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads with an arrow. And another grows back in its place. He cuts another. It grows back. Over and over. The story is telling you something with that. Many teachers read the ten heads as the ten things that keep growing back in all of us: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, jealousy, and the rest. Lists differ. The point doesn't. You can cut one down, and it comes back tomorrow. Which is why this lesson doesn't ask you to kill all ten today. It asks something smaller, and more honest. Look at your own. Pick one. And say its name.
screen: `SCHOLAR, DEVOTEE, MUSICIAN, KING.` · `THE ONE WHO MADE THE WORLDS CRY OUT.` · `CUT ONE HEAD. ANOTHER GROWS.` · `TEN HEADS: THE THINGS THAT GROW BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle. Picture ten heads, and don't be afraid of them. They're yours. Anger. Wanting more. Pride. Jealousy. Fear. Laziness. The need to be right. Whatever yours are. Let them line up. Now pick just one, the one that showed up most this week. Look it in the face. Don't fight it. Just say its name, quietly, inside. When it grows back, and it will, you'll recognize it faster. The bell holds the time.
Ravana rides out. The great, learned, ten-headed king, out of people to send, finally facing Rama himself.
Your line: name a head. Today, when one of yours shows up, anger, pride, whatever it is, say its name to yourself. Naming it is the first arrow. Day sixty-five.

66.title: The last arrow
66.hook: Agastya's mantra; the sun; Ravana falls
66.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant the Aditya Hridayam, the hymn Agastya teaches Rama, at sunrise or before difficult undertakings; Ravana's defeat is celebrated at Dussehra (Vijayadashami), when effigies of Ravana are burned in many towns.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana rides out, and the heads that kept growing back. Your line was name a head. Which one did you name? Day sixty-six.

You know the feeling at the end of something long. The last week of a hard job. The last night in the hospital. The last exam. You're so tired you can't feel whether you're winning. The fight between Rama and Ravana has gone on and on. The gods have sent Rama a chariot, Indra's own, driven by Indra's charioteer, Matali. Ravana's heads keep growing back. And Rama, in Valmiki's telling, is worn out, and worried. Then an old sage walks onto the battlefield. Agastya. And instead of a weapon, he gives Rama words.
screen: `THE END OF SOMETHING LONG.` → `HEADS THAT KEEP GROWING BACK.` → `A SAGE WALKS ONTO THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Agastya teaches Rama a hymn to the sun. It's called the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun. Praise the sun, the sage tells him, the one who lights every world and wakes every living thing. Recite this, and fear and grief will leave you. So, in the middle of a war, Rama stops. He looks at the sun. He recites the hymn, and in the story, strength comes back into him. People still chant this hymn today, before exams, before surgery, before hard days. The same words a tired prince heard on a battlefield. Then Matali, the charioteer, speaks up. Remember the weapon made by Brahma, he says. The time has come. And Rama takes out an arrow given to him long before: the brahmastra, the weapon of the creator himself. He sets it to the bow and releases it. It strikes Ravana in the chest, in the heart, and the king of Lanka falls from his chariot. The gods rain flowers. The war is over. Later tellings add a detail many people know: that Ravana kept a store of nectar in his navel, and Vibhishana told Rama where to aim. Valmiki's version doesn't have it; there the weapon itself does the work. Both agree on what matters. The last arrow didn't come from trying harder. It came after Rama stopped, turned toward the light, and steadied himself. And then something just as important: it ends. Wars in stories can feel endless. This one had a last day. Most long fights in a life do too.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `RAMA STOPS AND TURNS TO THE LIGHT.` · `THE BRAHMASTRA: THE LAST ARROW.` · `RAVANA FALLS. IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and if you can see daylight, turn toward it, or picture the sun on your face. Think of a long fight that finally ended for you. An illness, a hard season, a conflict with someone, a year you thought would never finish. It did. Let yourself feel that it's over, if you never stopped long enough to feel it. And if you're in the middle of one now, just take this one thing from Rama: stop for a moment, turn toward the light, and breathe. It will end. The bell holds the time.
The last arrow. A hymn to the sun, a weapon made by Brahma, and the end of the war in Lanka.
Your line: it ends. Today, if you're in something long, look up at the sky once, and remind yourself: it ends. Day sixty-six.

67.title: Mandodari's lament
67.hook: Ravana's queen weeps; even the villain is mourned
67.howItsDone: Mandodari is remembered in Hindu tradition as a wise and virtuous queen and is named in a well-known Sanskrit verse listing five revered women, the panchakanya, which many people recite in the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last arrow, the hymn to the sun, and Ravana falling from his chariot. Your line was it ends. Did you look up once? Day sixty-seven.

When a notorious person dies, the internet celebrates. The jokes arrive within minutes. And somewhere, off-camera, there's a woman sitting on a kitchen floor who has just lost her husband. The war is over. The monkeys are cheering. Ravana lies on the battlefield. And out through the gates of Lanka come the women of the palace, weeping, running to his body. At the front of them is his chief queen. Mandodari. And the Ramayana, a story that spent weeks building Ravana up as the enemy, stops everything to let her speak.
screen: `THE JOKES ARRIVE IN MINUTES.` → `THE WOMEN RUN FROM THE GATES.` → `THE STORY LETS HER SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Mandodari is the daughter of Maya, the great architect of the demons, and in the tradition she is wise and good. More than once she begged Ravana to send Sita back. He wouldn't listen. Now she kneels by his body and grieves, and her lament is one of the most moving passages in the poem. She remembers his greatness: the king who conquered the gods, who made the worlds tremble. She can't believe he's lying in the dust. She tells him, in effect: I warned you. Your desire for another man's wife is what killed you. And in the same breath, she weeps for him with her whole heart. She doesn't pretend he was innocent. She doesn't pretend she didn't love him. Both are true at once. Then Rama does something just as striking. Vibhishana, Ravana's brother, hesitates to perform the funeral rites: why honor a man who did such wrong? And Rama tells him, in Valmiki's telling, that hostility ends at death. The fight is over. He was your brother. Give him his rites. And Ravana is cremated with the honors of a king. Here's the thing the story knows, and it's not easy. Every villain was somebody's son, somebody's husband, somebody's father. The Ramayana doesn't let you cheer at a funeral. Many Hindus remember Mandodari among five women honored in a well-known verse, next to Ahalya, Draupadi and Tara. Her grief is honored, not mocked. Compassion for the fallen doesn't excuse anything. It just refuses to forget that someone loved him.
screen: `MANDODARI BEGGED HIM TO LISTEN.` · `I WARNED YOU. AND I LOVED YOU.` · `HOSTILITY ENDS AT DEATH.` · `EVERY VILLAIN WAS SOMEBODY'S.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of someone who fell. Someone in the news, someone in your family, someone who did real harm and paid for it. Don't excuse what they did. Just picture, for a moment, the person who loved them. A mother. A husband. A child. What are they feeling tonight? Let that sit next to everything else you know. You can hold both: what was wrong, and the grief. If you pray, you can hold those mourners in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Mandodari's lament. Ravana's queen, kneeling by his body, grieving the king she warned and still loved.
Your line: someone loved him. Today, before you join in on anyone's downfall, remember there's someone at home who's grieving. Day sixty-seven.

68.title: The fire
68.hook: Sita walks into the flame and out
68.carry: the tradition argues about this too
68.howItsDone: Sita's trial by fire is told and debated openly in Hindu homes, temples and scholarship; devotional tellings such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas present a shadow Sita, while many readers, poets and women's song traditions have long questioned the scene from Sita's side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mandodari's lament, Ravana's queen grieving the man she warned. Your line was someone loved him. Did you remember the mourners? Day sixty-eight.

This is the scene people stop at. The war is won. Sita is brought out of Lanka, after all those months in the garden, refusing Ravana every single day. The whole army crowds around to see her. She comes to Rama. This is the reunion the entire story has been running toward. And it goes wrong. Today we're not going to tidy this one up. We're going to tell it straight, and then tell you what people in the tradition have said about it, because they've been arguing about this scene for a very long time.
screen: `THE REUNION THE STORY RAN TOWARD.` → `AND IT GOES WRONG.` → `WE WON'T TIDY THIS ONE UP.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's telling, Rama speaks coldly, in front of everyone. He says he fought to wipe out the insult to his name, and that since she lived in another man's house, he can't simply take her back. She's free to go wherever she likes. Sita is stunned. Then she answers him, and her answer is magnificent: her heart was always his; what Ravana did to her body was done by force; how could he speak to her like a common man? And she turns to Lakshmana and tells him to build a fire. She walks into the flames. And the fire god, Agni, rises out of them carrying her unharmed, and declares her pure. Rama says he never doubted her; he did it, he says, so the world would have no doubt. That's the text. It's called agni pariksha: the trial by fire. Now, how the tradition reads it. Tulsidas, in the Ramcharitmanas, tells it differently: before the abduction, the real Sita was placed in the fire's keeping, and a shadow Sita was the one taken; the fire only gives the real one back. Many devotees take comfort in that. Others read Valmiki's scene as a king bowing to public opinion, and hold that as a flaw, or a tragedy, or a test of dharma under pressure. And for centuries, women have sung and retold this story from Sita's side, questioning Rama, like the sixteenth-century Bengali poet Chandrabati. Some scholars also point out that a still harder chapter, Sita's later banishment, comes in a book many consider a later addition. None of these voices is outside Hinduism. They're all inside it. That's the thing to carry: this tradition doesn't ask you to stop asking.
screen: `RAMA SPEAKS COLDLY, IN PUBLIC.` · `SITA ANSWERS, AND WALKS INTO THE FIRE.` · `AGNI CARRIES HER OUT.` · `SHADOW SITA, FLAW, OR TEST? ALL INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Don't try to decide what the scene means. Picture Sita, walking toward the fire, with her back straight. Picture Rama, watching. Let yourself feel whatever you feel: anger, confusion, awe, sadness. All of those have been felt by people who love this story. Now hold the question gently, like something you'll carry, not solve. If there's someone you could talk this through with, a parent, a friend, someone who grew up with the Ramayana, let their face come to mind. The bell holds the time.
Agni pariksha. The trial by fire. Sita walks into the flame and out, and the argument about it has never stopped.
Your line: the tradition argues about this too. Today, ask one person what they think of this scene, and listen more than you talk. Day sixty-eight.

69.title: The return
69.hook: lamps lit across Ayodhya; the night the whole country lights up
69.howItsDone: At Diwali, on the new-moon night of the month of Kartika, Hindus light rows of clay lamps (diyas) on doorsteps, windows and rooftops; in much of north India the festival is celebrated as Rama's return to Ayodhya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: agni pariksha, the trial by fire, and a scene the tradition still argues about. Your line was the tradition argues about this too. Did you ask someone what they think? Day sixty-nine.

Fourteen years. Think what fourteen years is. A child born the week Rama left would be a teenager now. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb into the Pushpaka, the flying chariot that belonged to Ravana, and head north. As they fly, Rama points down and shows Sita everything they've been through: there's the bridge. There's where Jatayu fell. There's Kishkindha. There's the forest where we lived. And far away, in a village outside Ayodhya, a man has been waiting the whole time, sleeping on the ground, ruling with a pair of sandals on the throne. His brother Bharata.
screen: `FOURTEEN YEARS.` → `THE FLYING CHARIOT HEADS NORTH.` → `BHARATA, STILL WAITING.`

segments.voice: Rama sends Hanuman ahead, flying, to tell Bharata they're coming. Why send word first? Because, in the story, Bharata had made a vow: if Rama didn't come back the day the fourteen years ended, he would give up his life. And the day has come. Hanuman finds him, thin, in bark clothes, hair matted, living like a hermit to match his brother in the forest. Rama is coming, Hanuman says. And Bharata's joy is so great he can hardly speak. Then the whole city pours out to meet the flying chariot. The brothers embrace. And here's where one of the biggest festivals in the world comes in. Tradition says that when Rama came home, the people of Ayodhya lit lamps: on doorsteps, on walls, along the rooftops, in every window, to welcome him, and to light the way home. Rows and rows of little clay lamps. In Sanskrit, a row of lamps is dipavali: dipa, a lamp, and avali, a row. Say it the way it's said all over India: Diwali. Valmiki describes Ayodhya's great celebration. The lamps, for most people, come from the way the story has been lived: every autumn, on the darkest night of the month, hundreds of millions of people light them again. Not all Hindus connect Diwali mainly with Rama; other regions tell other stories, and we'll hear some on another day. But in much of north India, this is the night. And here's the thing the story knows. Every little clay lamp on every windowsill, every year, is that night again. You don't remember it. You repeat it. Somebody's coming home. Light the way.
screen: `HANUMAN FLIES AHEAD TO BHARATA.` · `THE BROTHERS EMBRACE.` · `DIPAVALI: A ROW OF LAMPS.` · `EVERY LAMP, EVERY YEAR, IS THIS NIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a lamp, light it. If you don't, turn on one small light, or just picture a clay lamp on a windowsill. Look at the flame. Now think of someone who's been away. Someone who left for a long time, or someone you're still waiting for. A child at college. A friend who drifted. A parent far away. Picture them walking up the street at night, and your light in the window, showing them where home is. Just hold the light for them. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. From dipavali, a row of lamps: the night Ayodhya lit up to bring Rama home.
Your line: every lamp is this night. Tonight, leave one light on for someone who's coming home, even if it's just you. Day sixty-nine.

70.title: After
70.hook: the coronation; the sandals come down; what a serial leaves behind
70.howItsDone: Images of Rama's coronation (Rama pattabhishekam), with Sita beside him and Hanuman at his feet, hang in many Hindu homes; at some Ramayana readings and recitations a seat is left for Hanuman, who many believe is present wherever the story is told.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, the row of lamps that lit Rama home. Your line was every lamp is this night. Did you leave a light on? Day seventy.

You know the feeling when a series you've watched for weeks ends. The last episode. The credits. And then a strange quiet, like someone moved out. Five weeks ago, we started with an old king who had no sons. Then four boys, a bow nobody could lift, Sita choosing. Kaikeyi's two wishes. Fourteen years. A brother who put sandals on a throne. A golden deer, a line in the dust, an old bird who tried. Shabari's berries. A bridge, a squirrel, a foot nobody could move, a giant who woke, ten heads, a fire. Lamps. Today, the last episode.
screen: `THE LAST EPISODE.` → `FROM A KING WITH NO SONS...` → `...TO A CITY FULL OF LAMPS.`

segments.voice: Remember the sandals? Fourteen years ago, Bharata refused the throne and set Rama's sandals on it, and ruled as their servant. Now, in the story, he brings them back and places them on Rama's feet himself. I've kept your kingdom, he says, in effect; here it is. That's the image many Hindus hold of this day: a brother handing back what was never his. Then the coronation. Rama sits on the throne with Sita beside him, the brothers around them, and Hanuman at his feet. It's one of the most painted scenes in India, and you've probably seen it without knowing. And the story says Rama's reign was a time when there was no fear, no untimely death, when the rains came on time. People still say Ram Rajya, the rule of Rama, to mean a just and peaceful society, and people still argue about what that should look like. Valmiki's story doesn't stop cleanly here. There's another book after this one, with some of the hardest chapters in the whole Ramayana, and we'll meet them later on the path. But this serial ends at the coronation, the way many families' tellings do. So what does a serial leave behind? The Ramayana answers that itself. Near the end of the Uttara Kanda, Hanuman is offered a boon, and he asks for one thing: to stay alive on earth for as long as the story of Rama is told. Many Hindus believe he's still here. Listening. Wherever the Ramayana is read, some leave an empty seat for him. The ending isn't really the end. The story stays, as long as someone tells it.
screen: `THE SANDALS COME DOWN.` · `THE CORONATION, HANUMAN AT HIS FEET.` · `RAM RAJYA: NO FEAR.` · `AS LONG AS THE STORY IS TOLD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of something that ended recently: a chapter, a job, a friendship, a season of life, even a show you loved. Don't rush past it into what's next. Let the quiet after it be there. Now ask: what stayed? A lesson. A person. A habit. A line you still say. Let one thing come up. Then think of one character from these five weeks who stayed with you. Jatayu. Shabari. The squirrel. Let them sit with you a moment. The bell holds the time.
After. The sandals come down, the king is crowned, and Hanuman stays as long as the story is told.
Your line: the story stays. Today, tell one part of the Ramayana to someone who hasn't heard it. That's how it stays. Tomorrow, a new story, and a much bigger family. Day seventy.
